or_meth_lab_boulder.blurb: A single prominent boulder in the Garden Boulders cluster of the Willamette Valley, with a big overhanging prow that stands out from the road. It is a pure bouldering stop with close to thirty problems, and the pad count matters: the taller lines are around 15 feet and want several pads plus spotters. The grades lean hard. A few easy problems sit at the bottom end, then the bulk of the circuit runs from the high V7s through V9, topped by a V10. The sharpest concentration of classic lines is around the back side of the boulder, so a strong crew with plenty of pads gets the most out of it.

or_hanging_gardens.blurb: One of the larger walls on Broughton Bluff, the basalt crag near Troutdale where the Columbia Gorge opens out. This section is mostly crack and trad climbing, with only a handful of bolted lines among its roughly thirty routes. The wall is known for short, stacked pitches that make two- and three-pitch outings possible, though the whole thing is modest in height. Grades are friendly for an urban crag: a good number of routes in the 5.9 to 5.10 range, a few easier ones, and a thin tail of harder leads, with a single route far above the rest. Moss and seepage linger well into spring.

or_left_side.blurb: The left-hand wing of Northern Point at Smith Rock, reached by dropping through the approach gully and heading left. The walls are short basalt faces and cracks, a mix of bolted lines and trad leads, with a few top-ropes possible from the rim above. Difficulty is centered on the 5.11s, with a scattering of easier trad climbs around 5.7 to 5.9 and a run of 5.12s and low 5.13s for strong climbers. Shade arrives in the afternoon, which makes it a useful escape from the heat that bakes the larger faces nearby. Expect sport routes to outnumber trad here by a fair margin.

or_northern_end_the.blurb: The far north section of Trout Creek, a high basalt crag above the Deschutes River in central Oregon. The line is a long run of columnar pillars, and the climbing is entirely natural protection: cracks of every width, with bolts found only at the tops. This is the gentler end of the crag. Most of the roughly thirty routes fall between 5.8 and 5.10, with a few easier lines on the tilted pillars and a couple of 5.11s. The rock is rough and grippy, so tape is useful, and the pillars here face north and can carry lichen. It suits climbers stepping up to crack leading.
or_northern_end_the.approach: From the day-use area, follow the old road upstream along the river, then take the steep switchbacking trail up the slope to the foot of the pillars.

or_north_face.blurb: The north wall of Brogan Spire, reached on foot from the Marsupials side of Smith Rock. It is a sport-only face of nearly thirty single-pitch routes, and it is a venue for strong climbers: the bulk of the lines sit in the 5.12s and low 5.13s, with a few harder ones above and just a small handful of easier warm-ups in the 5.9 to 5.11 range. The stone is dense and very hard, and the best routes are steep and sustained. Plan on a real hike in. It is a poor choice for a beginner day.
